slides.title: AST 102: Galaxies
body_text: Our galaxy and the others
Dr. Alex Morgan
slides.speaker_notes: Sky report: look for the Andromeda galaxy from a dark site this week.

slides.title: The Milky Way From Inside
body_text: A faint band of light across the sky
It is the disk of our galaxy seen edge-on from within
We see more stars along the disk than above or below it
slides.speaker_notes: Standing in a forest: trees all around the horizon, open sky overhead.

slides.title: Disk, Bulge, Halo
body_text: Disk: about 100,000 light-years across, with gas, dust and young stars
Bulge: a thick central concentration of older stars
Halo: a sparse sphere of old stars and globular clusters
slides.speaker_notes: A few hundred billion stars in all, and a supermassive black hole at the very center.

slides.title: The Sun's Orbit
body_text: About 26,000 light-years (8 kpc) from the center
Orbital speed: about 230 km/s
One orbit: about 230 million years
slides.speaker_notes: The center is toward Sagittarius, hidden behind dust in visible light.

slides.title: Island Universes
body_text: Faint spiral nebulae turned out to be separate galaxies
The Andromeda galaxy is about 2.5 million light-years away
Hundreds of billions of galaxies in the observable universe
slides.speaker_notes: Andromeda is the most distant object most people can see without a telescope.

slides.title: Galaxy Types
body_text: Spiral: disk, arms and bulge; gas and young stars (the Milky Way, Andromeda)
Elliptical: smooth and oval; old stars, little gas
Irregular: no clear shape; often gas-rich (the Magellanic Clouds)
Barred spirals have a bar through the center; the Milky Way is one
slides.speaker_notes: Sorting activity: thirty galaxy images into three piles. Argue about the hard ones.

slides.title: Color Tells Age
body_text: Blue light comes from young, massive, short-lived stars
Red-yellow light comes from old, low-mass stars
Spiral arms are blue; ellipticals are red-yellow
slides.speaker_notes: If massive blue stars are present, stars formed in the last few million years.

slides.title: Rotation Curves
body_text: Plot orbital speed against distance from the center
Expected from visible matter: speeds falling off far from the center
Observed: speeds stay roughly flat far beyond the visible disk
Measured with the radio emission of hydrogen gas
slides.speaker_notes: Ball on a string: a faster swing at the same radius needs a stronger pull. Flat curves need more mass.

slides.title: The Dark Matter Halo
body_text: The extra mass is called dark matter
It emits and absorbs no light; we detect it only through gravity
About five times as much dark matter as ordinary matter
It forms a large halo around each galaxy
slides.speaker_notes: Other evidence agrees: galaxy clusters and gravitational lensing.

slides.title: What Could Dark Matter Be?
body_text: Not dark gas or dust: those would block or emit light
Not enough dim stars or black holes to account for it
Most likely a kind of particle not yet detected
Still an open question
slides.speaker_notes: Be clear about what is known: that it is there. Not what it is.
